claim: Efficient protein targeting to the inner nuclear membrane depends on nucleotide hydrolysis.
source: Using a visual in vitro assay we previously showed that efficient protein targeting to the INM depends on nucleotide hydrolysis.
evidence: The abstract states this finding was shown in previous work using a visual in vitro assay.

claim: INM targeting is GTP-dependent.
source: We now reveal that INM targeting is GTP-dependent.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a new finding from the current study.

claim: Atlastins sustain efficient targeting of proteins to the INM by their continued activity in preserving ER topology.
source: Exploiting in vitro reconstitution and in vivo analysis of INM targeting, we establish that Atlastins, membrane-bound GTPases of the ER, sustain the efficient targeting of proteins to the INM by their continued activity in preserving ER topology.
evidence: The abstract states this was established through in vitro reconstitution and in vivo analysis.

claim: When ER topology is altered, the long-range diffusional exchange of proteins in the ER network is diminished.
source: When ER topology is altered, the long-range diffusional exchange of proteins in the ER network and targeting efficiency to the INM are diminished.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from the study.

claim: When ER topology is altered, targeting efficiency to the INM is diminished.
source: When ER topology is altered, the long-range diffusional exchange of proteins in the ER network and targeting efficiency to the INM are diminished.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from the study.

claim: Atlastins influence NPC biogenesis.
source: Highlighting the general importance of proper ER topology, we show that Atlastins also influence NPC biogenesis and timely exit of secretory cargo from the ER.
evidence: The abstract states this was shown in the study.

claim: Atlastins influence timely exit of secretory cargo from the ER.
source: Highlighting the general importance of proper ER topology, we show that Atlastins also influence NPC biogenesis and timely exit of secretory cargo from the ER.
evidence: The abstract states this was shown in the study.

claim: The ER is a continuous membrane system spread throughout the cytoplasm.
source: Although the ER is a continuous membrane system that is spread throughout the cytoplasm, it possesses structurally distinct domains such as the mostly perinuclear, ribosome-studded ER sheets or the dense reticular network of peripheral ER tubules (Chen et al., 2013; Friedman and Voeltz, 2011; McNew et al., 2013; Shibata et al., 2006; Westrate et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The ER possesses structurally distinct domains including perinuclear ribosome-studded ER sheets and dense reticular networks of peripheral ER tubules.
source: Although the ER is a continuous membrane system that is spread throughout the cytoplasm, it possesses structurally distinct domains such as the mostly perinuclear, ribosome-studded ER sheets or the dense reticular network of peripheral ER tubules (Chen et al., 2013; Friedman and Voeltz, 2011; McNew et al., 2013; Shibata et al., 2006; Westrate et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: CLIMP63 is enriched in ER sheets.
source: The characteristic morphology of these ER domains is generated and maintained by proteins that partition into them; exemplified by the enrichment of the luminal ER spacing protein CLIMP63 in ER sheets and of the membrane curvature-inducing proteins of the reticulon and DP1/Yop1p families in ER tubules and at the edges of ER sheets (Lin et al., 2012; Shibata et al., 2010; Voeltz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Reticulon and DP1/Yop1p family proteins are enriched in ER tubules and at the edges of ER sheets.
source: The characteristic morphology of these ER domains is generated and maintained by proteins that partition into them; exemplified by the enrichment of the luminal ER spacing protein CLIMP63 in ER sheets and of the membrane curvature-inducing proteins of the reticulon and DP1/Yop1p families in ER tubules and at the edges of ER sheets (Lin et al., 2012; Shibata et al., 2010; Voeltz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The formation of the peripheral tubular ER network relies on homotypic membrane fusion mediated by GTPases of the Atlastin family.
source: The formation of the peripheral, tubular ER network relies on homotypic membrane fusion mediated by GTPases of the Atlastin family (Hu et al., 2009; Moss et al., 2011; Orso et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Atlastins weave membranes together, establishing the polygonal ER that expands towards the cell periphery.
source: Atlastins weave membranes together, establishing the polygonal ER that expands all the way towards the cell periphery (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Atlastins and membrane-tubule stabilizing factors are sufficient for the formation and maintenance of the tubular ER network in vitro.
source: In vitro, Atlastins and membrane-tubule stabilizing factors are sufficient for the formation and maintenance of the tubular ER network (Powers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ER network formation in living cells is supported by microtubules and RabGTPase-dependent growth of new membrane tubules.
source: In living cells, ER network formation is further supported by microtubules and RabGTPase-dependent growth of new membrane tubules (Audhya et al., 2007; English and Voeltz, 2013; Gerondopoulos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The nuclear envelope is formed by a specialized ER membrane sheet that surrounds and protects chromatin.
source: The boundary of the nuclear compartment - the nuclear envelope (NE) - is formed by a specialized ER membrane sheet that surrounds and protects chromatin (Anderson and Hetzer, 2008; Ungricht and Kutay, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The inner and outer nuclear membranes possess distinct protein compositions.
source: Reflecting functional specialization of the two NE lipid bilayers, the inner and outer nuclear membranes (INM and ONM) possess a distinct protein composition, even though both membranes are joined at numerous sites to form membranous pores.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nuclear envelope structure.

claim: The INM contains a unique set of membrane proteins that interact with nuclear lamins and chromatin.
source: Compared to the ONM and the ER, the INM contains a unique set of membrane proteins that interact with nuclear lamins and chromatin, thereby playing a critical role in nuclear organization and genome regulation (de Las Heras et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: INM proteins play a critical role in nuclear organization and genome regulation.
source: Compared to the ONM and the ER, the INM contains a unique set of membrane proteins that interact with nuclear lamins and chromatin, thereby playing a critical role in nuclear organization and genome regulation (de Las Heras et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Targeting of newly synthesized integral membrane proteins from the ER to the INM occurs within a system of continuous membranes.
source: Targeting of newly synthesized integral membrane proteins from the ER to the INM occurs within a system of continuous membranes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about INM targeting.

claim: Membrane proteins must pass through nuclear pore complexes to reach the INM.
source: To reach the INM, membrane proteins must pass through nuclear pore complexes (NPCs), which control nucleo-cytoplasmic exchange.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about INM targeting.

claim: The diffusion-retention model posits that proteins diffuse from the ER to the INM where they accumulate due to interactions with nuclear retention partners.
source: The initially proposed 'diffusion-retention model' posits that proteins diffuse from the ER to the INM, where they accumulate due to interactions with nuclear retention partners (Powell and Burke, 1990; Soullam and Worman, 1995).
evidence: This is a description of a model from prior literature, supported by citations.

claim: Energy-dependent enrichment of a reporter protein at the INM in human cells challenged the diffusion-retention model.
source: However, both the energy-dependent enrichment of a reporter protein at the INM in human cells (Ohba et al., 2004) and the description of transport receptor-mediated import of the yeast proteins Heh1 and 2 (King et al., 2006; Meinema et al., 2011) challenged this model, suggesting that INM targeting of the studied proteins may occur by an active process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Transport receptor-mediated import of yeast proteins Heh1 and Heh2 challenged the diffusion-retention model.
source: However, both the energy-dependent enrichment of a reporter protein at the INM in human cells (Ohba et al., 2004) and the description of transport receptor-mediated import of the yeast proteins Heh1 and 2 (King et al., 2006; Meinema et al., 2011) challenged this model, suggesting that INM targeting of the studied proteins may occur by an active process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Kinetic analyses and mathematical modeling affirmed that diffusion and retention sufficiently explain the targeting of several INM proteins in human cells.
source: Yet, recent kinetic analyses and mathematical modeling of protein sorting to the INM affirmed that diffusion and retention sufficiently explain the targeting of several INM proteins in human cells (Boni et al., 2015; Ungricht et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: INM targeting of investigated INM proteins is independent of the nucleo-cytoplasmic transport machinery.
source: Biochemical reconstitution further revealed that INM targeting of the investigated INM proteins is independent of the nucleo-cytoplasmic transport machinery (Ungricht et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Depletion of nucleoside triphosphates affected the efficiency of INM protein targeting.
source: Still, depletion of nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) affected the efficiency of INM protein targeting, which seems, at first glance, to contradict a diffusion-retention based mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work.

claim: Energy depletion induced changes in ER network topology.
source: At the same time, however, energy depletion also induced changes in ER network topology and reduced the long-range diffusional exchange of proteins in the ER (Ungricht et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Energy depletion reduced the long-range diffusional exchange of proteins in the ER.
source: At the same time, however, energy depletion also induced changes in ER network topology and reduced the long-range diffusional exchange of proteins in the ER (Ungricht et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NE enrichment of LBR(1-245)-GFP and SUN2-GFP was severely compromised upon addition of 0.3 mM GTPγS.
source: Strikingly, NE enrichment of both LBR and SUN2 was severely compromised upon addition of 0.3 mM GTPγS, comparable to the levels attained upon depletion of NTPs by apyrase (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NE enrichment of LBR(1-245)-GFP could be fully reconstituted by the mere addition of GTP to semi-permeabilized cells.
source: Remarkably, NE enrichment of LBR(1-245)-GFP could be fully reconstituted by the mere addition of GTP to semi-permeabilized cells, comparable to the levels obtained in presence of a complete energy regenerating system (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Addition of ATP did not suffice to support NE accumulation of LBR(1-245)-GFP beyond levels achieved by addition of buffer alone.
source: In contrast, addition of ATP did not suffice to support NE accumulation of LBR(1-245)-GFP beyond levels achieved by addition of buffer alone.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiment described in the text.

claim: Efficient enrichment of membrane proteins at the INM requires the enzymatic contribution of a GTPase present in the semi-permeabilized cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that efficient enrichment of membrane proteins at the INM requires the enzymatic contribution of a GTPase present in the semi-permeabilized cells, indicating that the GTPase in question may reside in the ER or nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results described.

claim: ER mobility of 2xRFP-tev-LBR(1-245)-GFP in semi-permeabilized cells was drastically compromised in the presence of GTPγS.
source: In line with the INM targeting defects, ER mobility of 2xRFP-tev-LBR(1-245)-GFP in semi-permeabilized cells supplemented with HeLa cell extract and energy was drastically compromised in the presence of GTPγS, but was unaffected by ATPγS (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ER mobility of 2xRFP-tev-LBR(1-245)-GFP was unaffected by ATPγS.
source: In line with the INM targeting defects, ER mobility of 2xRFP-tev-LBR(1-245)-GFP in semi-permeabilized cells supplemented with HeLa cell extract and energy was drastically compromised in the presence of GTPγS, but was unaffected by ATPγS (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The diffusional mobility of Sec61β-GFP was strongly reduced upon treatment with 0.3 mM GTPγS.
source: Similar to INM-destined reporters, the diffusional mobility of the ER-resident membrane protein Sec61β-GFP was also strongly reduced upon treatment with 0.3 mM GTPγS, and was insensitive to the same concentration of ATPγS (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The diffusional mobility of Sec61β-GFP was insensitive to 0.3 mM ATPγS.
source: Similar to INM-destined reporters, the diffusional mobility of the ER-resident membrane protein Sec61β-GFP was also strongly reduced upon treatment with 0.3 mM GTPγS, and was insensitive to the same concentration of ATPγS (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the presence of GTPγS, loss of fluorescence of GFP-KDEL in the surrounding area was significantly delayed.
source: In the presence of GTPγS, loss of fluorescence in the surrounding area was significantly delayed and the fluorescence intensity on the opposite side of the nucleus even remained stable throughout the 12 min time course of the experiment (Figure 2D, lower panels and graph).
evidence: This is supported by FLIP experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the presence of GTPγS, fluorescence intensity of GFP-KDEL on the opposite side of the nucleus remained stable throughout the 12 min time course.
source: In the presence of GTPγS, loss of fluorescence in the surrounding area was significantly delayed and the fluorescence intensity on the opposite side of the nucleus even remained stable throughout the 12 min time course of the experiment (Figure 2D, lower panels and graph).
evidence: This is supported by FLIP experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GTPγS alters ER organization.
source: Taken together, the observed defects on diffusional exchange of ER lumenal and membrane proteins suggest that GTPγS alters ER organization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the FRAP and FLIP experimental results.

claim: When GTPγS was added after 30 min recovery, the mobile fraction of 2xRFP-tev-LBR(1-245)-GFP rapidly dropped below 40%.
source: Strikingly, when GTPγS was added after 30 min, the mobile fraction rapidly dropped below 40% (Figure 3B), comparable to the reduction in reporter mobility observed without recovery phase (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GTP hydrolysis is necessary to maintain the diffusional mobility of ER membrane proteins.
source: Thus, GTP hydrolysis is not merely required to repair the ER network post semi-permeabilization, but is necessary to maintain the diffusional mobility of ER membrane proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recovery experiments with GTPγS addition.

claim: When GTPγS was injected into U2OS cells, the dynamics of the ER network was severely compromised.
source: In contrast, when GTPγS was injected, the dynamics of the network was severely compromised. The characteristic polygon structure of the peripheral ER began to disappear within a few minutes, giving rise to sparsely connected bright membrane spots, potentially ER vesicles, and elongated tubules (Figure 3C and E, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3C and E and Video 2.

claim: The characteristic polygon structure of the peripheral ER began to disappear within a few minutes after GTPγS injection.
source: In contrast, when GTPγS was injected, the dynamics of the network was severely compromised. The characteristic polygon structure of the peripheral ER began to disappear within a few minutes, giving rise to sparsely connected bright membrane spots, potentially ER vesicles, and elongated tubules (Figure 3C and E, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3C and E and Video 2.

claim: Cells injected with GTPγS displayed a drastically reduced number of membrane attachment events compared to cells injected with GTP.
source: Cells injected with GTPγS displayed a drastically reduced number of events as compared to cells injected with GTP. Moreover, the number of successful attachments decreased from >80% in control cells to less than half in GTPγS injected cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of ER dynamics shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The number of successful membrane attachments decreased from >80% in control cells to less than half in GTPγS injected cells.
source: Cells injected with GTPγS displayed a drastically reduced number of events as compared to cells injected with GTP. Moreover, the number of successful attachments decreased from >80% in control cells to less than half in GTPγS injected cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of ER dynamics shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ATL2 and ATL3 are expressed in HeLa cells.
source: The Atlastin (ATL) family comprises three members in human cells, of which ATL2 and 3 are expressed in HeLa cells (Rismanchi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Depletion of ATL2 alone led to a striking reduction in targeting of both LBR(1-245)-GFP and SUN2-GFP.
source: Depletion of ATL2 alone led to a striking reduction in targeting of both LBR(1-245)-GFP and SUN2-GFP (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 3) and the expected changes in ER morphology, i.e. long, unbranched tubules in the peripheral ER (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: Depletion of ATL2 led to long, unbranched tubules in the peripheral ER.
source: Depletion of ATL2 alone led to a striking reduction in targeting of both LBR(1-245)-GFP and SUN2-GFP (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 3) and the expected changes in ER morphology, i.e. long, unbranched tubules in the peripheral ER (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Depletion of ATL3 using six different siRNA oligonucleotides had no obvious effect on NE accumulation in HeLa cells.
source: Surprisingly, depletion of ATL3 using six different siRNA oligonucleotides (knockdown efficiency ≥80%) had no obvious effect on NE accumulation (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) or ER morphology in HeLa cells (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: Depletion of ATL3 had no obvious effect on ER morphology in HeLa cells.
source: Surprisingly, depletion of ATL3 using six different siRNA oligonucleotides (knockdown efficiency ≥80%) had no obvious effect on NE accumulation (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) or ER morphology in HeLa cells (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Depletion of ATL2 in ATL3 KO cells led to severe defects in ER morphology with more long unbranched tubules and sparser connections compared to single depletion of ATL2.
source: Knock-down of ATL2 in ATL3 KO cells, though, led to severe defects in ER morphology with even more long unbranched tubules and sparser connections as compared to the single depletion of ATL2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Targeting of LBR(1-245)-GFP to the NE was efficient in ATL3 KO cells.
source: In agreement with the RNAi experiments (Figure S1), targeting of LBR(1-245)-GFP to the NE was efficient in ATL3 KO cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Depletion of ATL2 strongly reduced NE accumulation of LBR(1-245)-GFP after 45 min.
source: In contrast, depletion of ATL2 strongly reduced NE accumulation of LBR(1-245)-GFP after 45 min (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ATL2 depletion by RNAi reduced the mobility of the LBR reporter in the ER significantly.
source: In correlation with the INM targeting defect, ATL2 depletion by RNAi reduced the mobility of the reporter in the ER significantly, leading to a drop in both the size of the mobile fraction and apparent diffusion coefficient (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Knock-out of ATL3 alone had no effect on ER mobility of the LBR reporter.
source: Knock-out of ATL3 alone had no effect.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the FRAP experiments.

claim: Depletion of ATL2 in the ATL3 KO background further reduced the mobility of membrane protein reporters to a similar extent as competition with GTPγS.
source: However, depletion of ATL2 in the ATL3 KO background further reduced the mobility of the membrane protein reporters to a similar extent as competition with GTPγS (Figure 4D and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 2B.

claim: Overexpression of cytATL2-RFP in U2OS cells led to the formation of long unbranched tubules and a significant reduction in the number of polygons in the peripheral ER.
source: As expected, overexpression of cytATL2-RFP in U2OS cells led to the formation of long unbranched tubules and a significant reduction in the number of polygons in the peripheral ER compared to RFP alone or a cytATL mutant that abolishes dimerization (R244Q for cytATL2 and R213Q for cytATL3, (Byrnes and Sondermann, 2011)) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The ER of cells overexpressing cytATL2-RFP appeared to be significantly less dynamic than the ER of cells overexpressing cytATL2(R244Q)-RFP or RFP alone.
source: In addition, the ER of cells overexpressing cytATL2-RFP appeared to be significantly less dynamic than the ER of cells overexpressing cytATL2(R244Q)-RFP or RFP alone (Videos 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Videos 3-5.

claim: The number of successful attachments of ER tubules to neighboring membranes was reduced from 81% to 47% in cells overexpressing cytATL2-RFP.
source: The number of successful attachments of ER tubules to neighboring membranes was reduced from 81% to 47% (Figure 5B), reminiscent of the reduction observed in cells injected with GTPγS (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of ER dynamics shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Enrichment of LBR(1-245)-GFP at the NE was strongly impaired upon addition of wild-type cytATL2 or cytATL3.
source: Enrichment of LBR(1-245)-GFP at the NE was strongly impaired upon addition of wild-type cytATL2 or cytATL3, but was not affected by the addition of cytATL2(R244Q) or cytATL3(R213Q) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Enrichment of LBR(1-245)-GFP at the NE was not affected by the addition of cytATL2(R244Q) or cytATL3(R213Q).
source: Enrichment of LBR(1-245)-GFP at the NE was strongly impaired upon addition of wild-type cytATL2 or cytATL3, but was not affected by the addition of cytATL2(R244Q) or cytATL3(R213Q) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Rab7 and Rab11 were efficiently extracted from membranes of semi-permeabilized cells with 20 μM recombinant GDI.
source: Even though Rab7 and Rab11 were efficiently extracted from membranes of semi-permeabilized cells with 20 μM recombinant GDI (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), targeting of LBR(1-245)-GFP remained unaffected (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Targeting of LBR(1-245)-GFP remained unaffected by RabGDI treatment.
source: Even though Rab7 and Rab11 were efficiently extracted from membranes of semi-permeabilized cells with 20 μM recombinant GDI (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), targeting of LBR(1-245)-GFP remained unaffected (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The combination of RabGDI and cytATL2 did not further decrease targeting efficiency.
source: Also the combination of RabGDI and cytATL2 did not further decrease targeting efficiency, suggesting that Rabs are not involved in INM targeting or ER maintenance in the semi-permeabilized cell system.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Rabs are not involved in INM targeting or ER maintenance in the semi-permeabilized cell system.
source: Also the combination of RabGDI and cytATL2 did not further decrease targeting efficiency, suggesting that Rabs are not involved in INM targeting or ER maintenance in the semi-permeabilized cell system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RabGDI experiments.

claim: LBR(1-245)-SBP-GFP and LAP2β-SBP-GFP accumulated at the NE with different rates in living cells.
source: In agreement with the INM targeting kinetics that we had previously measured in semi-permeabilized cells (Ungricht et al., 2015), LBR(1-245)-SBP-GFP and LAP2β-SBP-GFP accumulated at the NE with different rates in living cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NE accumulation of both LBR(1-245)-SBP-GFP and LAP2β-SBP-GFP was delayed in cells overexpressing cytATL2-RFP.
source: Indeed, NE accumulation of both LBR(1-245)-SBP-GFP and LAP2β-SBP-GFP was delayed in cells overexpressing cytATL2-RFP (t1/2 of LBR(1-245) increased from ~12 min to ~25 min), whereas cells overexpressing cytATL2(R244Q)-RFP or RFP as negative controls displayed unaltered targeting kinetics (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The t1/2 of LBR(1-245) increased from ~12 min to ~25 min in cells overexpressing cytATL2-RFP.
source: Indeed, NE accumulation of both LBR(1-245)-SBP-GFP and LAP2β-SBP-GFP was delayed in cells overexpressing cytATL2-RFP (t1/2 of LBR(1-245) increased from ~12 min to ~25 min), whereas cells overexpressing cytATL2(R244Q)-RFP or RFP as negative controls displayed unaltered targeting kinetics (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cells overexpressing cytATL2(R244Q)-RFP or RFP displayed unaltered INM targeting kinetics.
source: Indeed, NE accumulation of both LBR(1-245)-SBP-GFP and LAP2β-SBP-GFP was delayed in cells overexpressing cytATL2-RFP (t1/2 of LBR(1-245) increased from ~12 min to ~25 min), whereas cells overexpressing cytATL2(R244Q)-RFP or RFP as negative controls displayed unaltered targeting kinetics (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Co-depletion of ATL2 and ATL3 causes an NPC biogenesis defect, manifesting by reduced staining of the NE and accumulation of nucleoporins in cytoplasmic structures.
source: Note that co-depletion of ATL2 and ATL3 causes an NPC biogenesis defect, manifesting by reduced staining of the NE and accumulation of nucleoporins in cytoplasmic structures.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunofluorescence data.

claim: Steady state levels of INM proteins at the NE are unaffected by Atlastin depletion in most unsynchronized interphase cells.
source: Alterations in ER morphology perturbed the efficient diffusional exchange of proteins in the ER network and affected the targeting kinetics of INM proteins. The kinetic delay in targeting of newly synthesized INM proteins induced by Atlastin depletion did not visibly affect the steady-state levels of endogenous LBR, LAP2β, SUN1, and emerin at the NE in the majority of unsynchronized interphase cells (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), likely because newly synthesized INM proteins present only a minor fraction of the total pool at a given time.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Twin pairs of cells 12 hr after release from thymidine block showed visible accumulation of INM proteins in the ER upon co-depletion of ATL2 and ATL3.
source: These twin pairs of cells showed a visible accumulation of INM proteins in the ER, exemplified by immunofluorescence analyses of LBR, LAP2β, SUN1, and emerin upon co-depletion of ATL2 and ATL3 (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: NPC biogenesis critically depends on targeting of membrane proteins to the NE.
source: Notably, NPC biogenesis is known to critically depend on targeting of membrane proteins to the NE (Antonin et al., 2005; Doucet et al., 2010; Talamas and Hetzer, 2011; Yavuz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Immunostaining of nucleoporins revealed their striking mislocalization into annulate lamellae upon co-depletion of ATL2 and ATL3.
source: Indeed, immunostaining of nucleoporins revealed their striking mislocalization into annulate lamellae – stacks of ER sheets that contain NPCs (Cordes et al., 1996) – upon co-depletion of ATL2 and ATL3 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mislocalization of nucleoporins was accompanied by a reduction in nucleoporin levels at the NE, indicative of a defect in chromatin-based NPC biogenesis.
source: This mislocalization was accompanied by a reduction in nucleoporin levels at the NE, indicative of a defect in chromatin-based NPC biogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the immunofluorescence observations.

claim: VSVG rapidly enriched at bright puncta within 1 min in control cells, consistent with VSVG accumulation at ER exit sites.
source: Kinetic measurements of VSVG trafficking from the ER to the Golgi showed that VSVG rapidly enriched at bright puncta within 1 min in control cells (see bright puncta in siCtr., Figure 7B), consistent with VSVG accumulation at ER exit sites.
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: VSVG accumulated in the Golgi complex within 5 min in control cells.
source: VSVG then accumulated in the Golgi complex within 5 min.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the VSVG trafficking experiments.

claim: At 15 min, VSVG started to be visible at the plasma membrane in control cells.
source: At 15 min, VSVG already started to be visible at the plasma membrane (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The enrichment of VSVG in the Golgi complex was delayed to a similar extent in cells depleted of ATL2 or both ATL2 and 3.
source: Strikingly, the enrichment of the reporter in the Golgi complex was delayed to a similar extent in cells depleted of ATL2 or both ATL2 and 3 but less so in ATL3-depleted cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the VSVG trafficking experiments.

claim: The enrichment of VSVG in the Golgi complex was delayed less in ATL3-depleted cells compared to ATL2-depleted cells.
source: Strikingly, the enrichment of the reporter in the Golgi complex was delayed to a similar extent in cells depleted of ATL2 or both ATL2 and 3 but less so in ATL3-depleted cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the VSVG trafficking experiments.

claim: The retardation in VSVG enrichment in the Golgi correlated with a delayed arrival of VSVG at ER exit sites.
source: This retardation correlated with a delayed arrival of VSVG at ER exit sites (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Only a kinetic delay in VSVG transport from the ER to the Golgi was observed, not a block in trafficking.
source: Note that we only observed a kinetic delay in VSVG transport from the ER to the Golgi but not a block in trafficking, explaining why ER exit of a temperature-sensitive mutant of VSVG studied at longer time intervals seemed unaffected by depletion or deletion of Atlastins in previous studies (Rismanchi et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and reconciles with prior literature.

claim: Nuclear import of soluble cargo depends on the RanGTPase system that generates a high concentration of RanGTP in the nucleus.
source: Nuclear import of soluble cargo depends on the RanGTPase system that generates a high concentration of RanGTP in the nucleus. Nuclear RanGTP is needed for the dissociation of import substrates from shuttling nuclear transport receptors (Görlich and Kutay, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Transport of SUN2 and LBR to the INM is not directly dependent on the RanGTPase system and the nucleo-cytoplasmic transport machinery for soluble cargo.
source: In contrast to import of soluble cargo, transport of SUN2 and LBR to the INM is not directly dependent on the RanGTPase system and the nucleo-cytoplasmic transport machinery for soluble cargo and not affected by addition of RanQ69L – a GTPase-deficient mutant of Ran that efficiently prevents importin-cargo interactions (Ungricht et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: De novo ER network formation in vitro using Xenopus egg extracts requires GTP.
source: Originally, it has been demonstrated that de novo ER network formation in vitro using Xenopus egg extracts requires GTP (Dreier and Rapoport, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: An in vitro reconstituted ER network disassembles upon addition of GTPγS.
source: Recent observations revealed that an in vitro reconstituted ER network disassembles upon addition of GTPγS (Powers et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GTP hydrolysis is needed to maintain ER network topology in semi-permeabilized and living human somatic cells.
source: Extending the latter finding, we demonstrate that GTP hydrolysis is needed to maintain ER network topology in semi-permeabilized and living human somatic cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: A requirement of GTP hydrolysis for efficient targeting of proteins to the INM arises from its need for the generation and maintenance of ER network topology.
source: Thus, a requirement of GTP hydrolysis for the efficient targeting of proteins to the INM arises from its need for the generation and maintenance of ER network topology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: ATL2 is a more potent fusogen than ATL3.
source: It is possible that ATL2 is a more potent fusogen than ATL3 as previously proposed (Hu et al., 2015) and/or that ATL3 is less abundant than ATL2 in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations and prior literature.

claim: ATL3 is less abundant than ATL2 in HeLa cells.
source: It is possible that ATL2 is a more potent fusogen than ATL3 as previously proposed (Hu et al., 2015) and/or that ATL3 is less abundant than ATL2 in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations.

claim: ATL3 function may become critical in the absence of ATL2.
source: The aggravated defects in ER morphology that we observed upon co-depletion of ATL2 and ATL3 suggest that ATL3 function may become critical in the absence of ATL2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-depletion experiments.

claim: Atlastins may form mixed dimers under conditions of excess recombinant protein.
source: The potent impairment of INM targeting by cytATL3 may, however, suggest that Atlastins form mixed dimers under those conditions using excess recombinant protein, similar to what has been observed before (Rismanchi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculation based on observations and prior literature.

claim: ATL3 is less aligned with microtubules compared to ATL2.
source: Compared to ATL2, ATL3 was found to be less aligned with microtubules (Rismanchi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ATL3 depletion might more specifically affect the organization of ER membrane domains relevant for timely ER exit.
source: It is thus conceivable that ATL3 depletion might more specifically affect the organization of ER membrane domains relevant for timely ER exit.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations.

claim: All Atlastins have been found associated with vesicular tubular clusters and the cis-Golgi.
source: Notably, all Atlastins have also been found associated with vesicular tubular clusters (VTCs) and the cis-Golgi.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The continuity and interconnectivity of the ER network is preserved by frequent homotypic membrane fusion events.
source: Despite its dynamic behavior and separation into structurally distinct domains, the continuity and interconnectivity of the ER network is preserved by frequent homotypic membrane fusion events.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The continuity of the ER aids the timely delivery of proteins to the INM.
source: For one, it may assure rapid flux of proteins and lipids from their site of synthesis to the site of function. Our study emphasizes that the continuity of the ER aids the timely delivery of proteins to the INM, thereby promoting the generation of a specific ER subdomain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: A well-connected ER assures unhindered diffusion of newly synthesized INM proteins to accompany nuclear growth and NE expansion during interphase.
source: A well-connected ER assures an unhindered diffusion of newly synthesized INM proteins to accompany the nuclear growth and NE expansion during interphase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study findings.

claim: The interconnected topology of the ER network is important for the timely exit of newly synthesized cargo into the secretory pathway.
source: The interconnected topology of the ER network is also important for the timely exit of newly synthesized cargo into the secretory pathway, as exemplified by the delayed trafficking of the model protein VSVG from the ER to the Golgi upon Atlastin depletion.
evidence: This is supported by the VSVG trafficking data.

claim: The ER remains intact during mitosis.
source: Even during mitosis, the ER remains intact (Ellenberg et al., 1997), despite the large-scale reorganization of the NE-ER network.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Interference with Atlastin function early during in vitro nuclear assembly abrogates NE formation.
source: Interestingly, interference with Atlastin function early during in vitro nuclear assembly abrogates NE formation, whereas Atlastin inhibition at a later phase impairs NE expansion (Wang et al., 2013), indicating that ER connectivity is important for nuclear reformation after mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Atlastin inhibition at a later phase of nuclear assembly impairs NE expansion.
source: Interestingly, interference with Atlastin function early during in vitro nuclear assembly abrogates NE formation, whereas Atlastin inhibition at a later phase impairs NE expansion (Wang et al., 2013), indicating that ER connectivity is important for nuclear reformation after mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ER connectivity is important for nuclear reformation after mitosis.
source: Interestingly, interference with Atlastin function early during in vitro nuclear assembly abrogates NE formation, whereas Atlastin inhibition at a later phase impairs NE expansion (Wang et al., 2013), indicating that ER connectivity is important for nuclear reformation after mitosis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior literature findings.

claim: INM proteins need to be recruited back to chromatin during late ana- and telophase to support chromatin enclosure by membranes and promote post-mitotic NPC assembly.
source: During nuclear reassembly, INM proteins need to be recruited back to chromatin during a very short time window in late ana- and telophase, not only to support chromatin enclosure by membranes but also to promote post-mitotic NPC assembly (Antonin et al., 2005; Mansfeld et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurons demand an intricate ER topology with a network of tubular projections and irregularly spaced cisternae reaching down along the axon.
source: Neurons demand for an intricate ER topology, with a network of tubular projections and irregularly spaced cisternae reaching down all along the axon (González and Couve, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The dimensions of the ER in neuronal cells might explain their vulnerability for mutations in ER shaping proteins.
source: The dimensions of the ER in neuronal cells might explain their vulnerability for mutations in ER shaping proteins and their demand for a potent fusogen as ATL1 (Li et al., 2017; Rismanchi et al., 2008; Summerville et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Changes in ER network topology influence trafficking of membrane proteins in small, non-neuronal cells.
source: Our study emphasizes how changes in ER network topology already influence trafficking of membrane proteins in small, non-neuronal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: Perturbations in ER morphology that cause subtle defects in protein trafficking are likely enhanced in neurons due to long axonal extensions.
source: Such perturbations in ER morphology that cause subtle defects in protein trafficking are likely enhanced applied to neurons due to the long axonal extensions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study findings.
